then.text: I am resting. In the mud. Do not tell the King.
Out at the end of the causeway, on the old camp island, a beacon flares in the reeds.

else.text: This causeway is closed by order of King William. Unless you know something of the rebels, peasant, move along.

then.text: A tall figure waits by the beacon, half reed, half mail, wholly unbothered by a thousand years.

else.text: The beacon roars up. Out of the reeds steps a warrior caked in fen mud, mail glinting, a long axe on his shoulder and a grin like a man who has never once lost an argument.
So. You beat Ivo. Good. I never managed it properly; I just kept escaping, which annoyed him more.
They call me Hereward the Wake. For a year I held this island against William the Conqueror with a few hundred fenmen and some very cross monks.
In the end the abbot showed the Normans a secret path. I slipped away into the reeds and was never caught. The fen keeps its own. Shall we see if you can keep me?

then.text: Hereward shoulders his axe and falls in beside you, as if he'd been waiting for a decent excuse to leave the island.

else.text: Hereward laughs, steps back into the reeds, and is simply gone. The beacon still burns. He'll be back; he always was.

fen_drainer.text: {greeting} In the 1630s the Earl of Bedford hired a Dutchman, Cornelius Vermuyden, to drain the Fens. He cut great straight rivers, like the Old and New Bedford, to rush the water out to the sea.
Windpumps did the lifting for two hundred years, then steam, then diesel, now electric. If the pumps all stopped, a lot of this would be under water again within a winter. No pressure on the pumps.

crane.text: A grey crane with a red cap struts through the reeds, bows to nobody in particular, and does a little dance. Four hundred years they were gone. It has a lot of dancing to catch up on.

fen_swanwatcher.text: Whooper swans from Iceland, Bewick's from Siberia. Every winter thousands land here on the washes. They fly further for their holidays than I do.

fen_tigerwitness.text: Big skies round here. Folk say we've got more sky than anywhere in England, on account of having nothing in the way of it.
I seen it once, the tiger. In the sugar beet. Big as a calf, stripy tail. My wife says it was the neighbour's ginger tom. My wife wasn't there.
